title: Robustness of the Verwey transition against remanent strain-induced defects in magnetite
authors: M. A. Gala, K. J. Grzywa, K. Komędera, R. Zalecki, A. Baczmański, Z. Kąkol, A. Pacanowska, C. M. N. Kumar, R. Rodriguez Lamas, C. Detlefs, C. Yildirim, C. Marin, J. Debray, G. Beutier, L. Ortega, A. Kozłowski, N. Barišić, J. E. Lorenzo, W. Tabiś
abstract: The Verwey transition in magnetite is a benchmark electronically driven phase transition that is highly sensitive to lattice imperfections and external perturbations. Doping, deviations from oxygen stoichiometry, and irradiation-induced point defects are known to lower the Verwey transition temperature, $T_{\rm V}$. By contrast, the role of remanent strain fields and extended defect structures generated by uniaxial stress has remained largely unexplored. Here we combine dark-field x-ray microscopy (DFXM) and ac magnetic susceptibility to determine how strain-induced defects affect the Verwey transition in stoichiometric single-crystalline magnetite after uniaxial compression and unloading. The DFXM measurements were performed on two samples compressed along the same $[011]$ direction: loading to $200~\mathrm{MPa}$ generated stable line-like defects and remanent strain fields, whereas loading beyond the fracture threshold produced denser defect networks and mechanical fracture. To test the effect of a different loading geometry, we also measured the ac susceptibility of a sample fractured by compression along $[001]$. Real-space DFXM imaging, lattice-orientation mapping, and residual strain mapping show substantial remanent structural disorder after compression. Nevertheless, neither the transition temperature $T_{\rm V}$ nor the sharpness of the transition changes measurably in any of the compressed or fractured samples. This behavior contrasts with the strong suppression of $T_{\rm V}$ by point-like disorder. Our results show that extended line-like defects and remanent strain fields produced by plastic deformation do not measurably perturb the macroscopic electronic ordering responsible for the Verwey transition, thereby distinguishing the effects of point defects from those of extended slip-related defects in magnetite.
summary: This experimental study investigates the robustness of the Verwey transition in magnetite when subjected to mechanical stress. By comparing the electronic transition signature with high-resolution imaging of strain-induced defects, the authors conclude that extended slip-related defects do not significantly alter the transition temperature. This work helps distinguish the physical mechanism by which point defects suppress the transition from that caused by extended lattice strain.
main_problem: To determine how remanent strain fields and extended defect structures, generated by uniaxial stress, affect the Verwey transition in magnetite.
main_result: The study found that extended line-like defects and remanent strain fields from plastic deformation do not measurably perturb the Verwey transition temperature, distinguishing their effect from point defects.
method: The researchers combined dark-field x-ray microscopy (DFXM) to map structural disorder and ac magnetic susceptibility measurements to track the electronic phase transition.
model_or_system: The physical system is stoichiometric single-crystalline magnetite ($	ext{Fe}_3	ext{O}_4$), a material known for its electronically driven Verwey transition, which is sensitive to lattice imperfections.
key_observables: Verwey transition temperature ($T_V$), transition sharpness, remanent structural disorder (line-like defects, strain fields), and lattice misorientation/strain maps.
important_parameters: Uniaxial stress (up to 200 MPa), temperature ramp rate ($\le 0.1$ K/min), and the comparison between point defects vs. extended defects.
main_assumptions: The study assumes that the observed structural disorder is primarily due to plastic deformation (slip-related) and that the electronic ordering responsible for $T_V$ is sensitive only to the type of disorder, not its density, if the disorder is extended.
figures_summary: Figures show DFXM contrast images comparing pristine, moderately compressed, and fractured samples, revealing substantial remanent structural disorder. Susceptibility curves confirm that $T_V$ remains unchanged across these mechanically altered samples.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the problem by noting the sensitivity of $T_V$ to point defects. It then details the experimental procedure involving uniaxial compression and subsequent DFXM/susceptibility measurements. The core of the paper presents the results showing structural disorder without corresponding changes in $T_V$, leading to the conclusion that extended defects are benign compared to point defects.
why_interesting: The work provides crucial experimental evidence distinguishing between the coupling mechanisms of different types of lattice disorder (point vs. extended) to the electronic ground state, which is fundamental to understanding correlated electron physics in transition metal oxides.

figures.caption: Figure 1. Uniaxial compression and magnetic characterization of magnetite. (a) Compression device consisting of a cylindrical steel housing and a central piston. (b) Magnetite sample mounted between ceramic posts with Stycast epoxy; purple arrows indicate the direction of applied uniaxial compression. (c) Real part of the ac susceptibility, χ′, for the pristine reference sample and for samples fractured by compression along [011] and [001] directions. Within experimental resolution, the Verwey transition temperature remains unchanged after compression and fracture.

Figure 2. Schematic of the DFXM setup at the ESRF ID03 beamline. A monochromatic x-ray beam illuminates the sam- ple, which is mounted on a goniometer. A selected Bragg reflection from the cubic {400} family is magnified by com- pound refractive lenses and imaged on a two-dimensional de- tector. Rocking and rolling scans probe lattice misorientation, while scans of 2θ probe local changes in lattice spacing. The DFXM end station at ID03 was relocated and upgraded from the former ID06-HXM instrument [24]. Schematic adapted from Ref. [25].

Figure 3. DFXM geometry used to image the compressed magnetite crystals. (a) Sample orientation relative to the incident x-ray beam. The sample was compressed along [011], with a (01¯1) surface exposed in the DFXM geometry. The cubic (400) reflection was selected for imaging. (b) Schematic of the DFXM optical layout in the box-beam geometry. The vertical direction of the recorded image corresponds to the sample thickness, and the x-ray objective inverts the image, reversing the front and rear sides of the sample.

Figure 4 shows detector images recorded near the max- imum of the (400) Bragg reflection for the pristine ref- erence crystal, the moderately compressed crystal, and the fractured crystal compressed along [011]. These im- ages are not full orientation or strain maps. Instead, they show the spatial distribution of diffracted intensity at the angular setting for which the largest part of the illuminated region satisfies the Bragg condition. They therefore provide a direct visual comparison of the ho- mogeneity of the diffracting volume in the three samples.
